evidenceAudit.scope: Approach to fever in children in India (beyond the neonatal period): definition, danger signs, assessment, investigations by fever duration and focus, antipyretics, first doses for life-threatening infection, admission, referral and discharge, built on the ICMR Fever in Children STW (October 2019).
findings: Fever definition (rectal 38.0°C or more; axillary above 37.5°C), assessment, danger signs, no tests for a well child with fever under 72 hours, essential and desirable tests for fever over 72 hours and over 7 days, clinical clues by feature, paracetamol 15 mg/kg, no empiric anti-TB treatment except suspected TB meningitis, referral and discharge criteria checked against the ICMR Fever in Children STW (October 2019).
First-dose ceftriaxone and artesunate doses from the ICMR AES in Children STW.
unverifiedSections: The ICMR workflow gives no paracetamol interval or maximum and does not mention ibuprofen; both are taken from the Gloucestershire children's analgesia guideline (2020).
The workflow does not split approach by age (under 3 months, 3–36 months); young infants who look toxic are treated as urgent.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Fever is the commonest reason children are brought to doctors in India. Most fevers are viral and self-limiting, but serious bacterial infections, malaria, dengue, enteric fever, scrub typhus, urinary infection and tuberculosis must not be missed. The ICMR approach is to assess how sick the child looks, look for a focus, treat danger signs at once, and use investigations only when they will change management: none for a well child with fever under 72 hours; blood count, smear and platelets after 72 hours; and a wider work-up for fever over 7 days (ICMR STW). Paracetamol treats discomfort; it does not treat the cause. Infants under 3 months and children with severe malnutrition may not mount a fever or localise infection, so their threshold for investigation and admission is lower.
keyMechanisms: Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) reset the hypothalamic set point.
Infection is the usual trigger; inflammatory and malignant causes are less common.
Young infants have immature immunity and localise infection poorly.
Prolonged fever suggests TB, enteric fever, abscess, autoimmune disease or malignancy.

symptoms: Localising symptoms: cough, dysuria, diarrhoea, headache, joint pain
Rash, joint pain or bleeding (dengue, chikungunya, meningococcaemia)
physicalSigns: Temperature: rectal 38.0°C or more, axillary above 37.5°C (ICMR STW)
Tachycardia, tachypnoea, prolonged capillary filling time
redFlags: Toxic appearance, lethargy, irritability or inconsolability (ICMR STW)
Fever over 14 days without a diagnosis (ICMR STW)
Rash with shock or organ dysfunction: meningococcaemia (ICMR STW)
precipitants: Viral infections, recent vaccination within 24 hours (ICMR STW)
Similar illness in family or neighbourhood (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fever with chills, pallor and splenomegaly in an endemic area; a positive smear or rapid diagnostic test settles it.
High fever, myalgia, rash, falling platelets and rising haematocrit; NS1 in the first 5 days or IgM later settles it.
Stepwise fever over 7 days with abdominal symptoms; blood culture settles it, Widal only after 7 days (ICMR STW).
Fever without focus in infants or with dysuria; clean-catch urine microscopy and culture settles it.

Prolonged fever with strawberry tongue, conjunctival injection, rash, peeling and lymphadenopathy (ICMR STW); echocardiography assesses the coronaries (see the Kawasaki disease topic for IVIG and aspirin).
Eschar, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia in the monsoon; scrub typhus IgM ELISA settles it.
Fever over 2 weeks with weight loss, cough or contact history; chest X-ray, Mantoux and Xpert settle it (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Vital signs, appearance, history including vaccination in last 24 hours and contacts (ICMR STW).
Full examination for a focus (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Comfort and fluids
actions: Paracetamol 15 mg/kg by any route and/or hydrotherapy for discomfort, not to reach a number (ICMR STW).
Avoid NSAIDs when dengue is possible; ibuprofen only for discomfort after paracetamol in a child over 3 months (Gloucestershire guideline).

clinicalManagement.title: Danger signs
actions: Lower temperature with paracetamol and tepid sponging (ICMR STW).
Manage life-threatening problems (airway, shock, seizures) (ICMR STW).
First antibiotic dose for suspected meningitis, severe pneumonia or severe malnutrition; antimalarial if malaria suspected (ICMR STW).
Shock: normal saline 20 mL/kg IV and reassess (ICMR AES STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Investigate by duration
actions: Well child, fever under 72 hours: no tests (ICMR STW).
Over 72 hours: blood count, smear, platelets; add RDT, NS1/IgM, blood and urine culture as indicated (ICMR STW).
Over 7 days: add Widal, TB tests (Mantoux, Xpert), HIV, autoimmune tests and imaging (ICMR STW).
Do not start empiric anti-TB treatment except for suspected TB meningitis (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Admit or refer
actions: Admit for ongoing care needs; refer to tertiary care for intensive care unit (ICU) needs, complex multi-system disease or complications (ICMR STW).
Discharge a well child with clear return advice: inability to feed, lethargy, breathing difficulty, rash, bleeding or fever beyond 3 days (usual practice).

vignette.text: Kabir, an 18-month-old boy from Patna, has had fever for 4 days. He is drinking but less playful, has no cough, diarrhoea or rash, and was fully vaccinated last month. Temperature is 39.2 °C axillary, pulse 150/min, respiratory rate 32/min and capillary refill under 2 seconds. Examination shows no focus. His mother has given him paracetamol syrup every 2 hours to keep the temperature down.

guidedApproach.title: Fever is a response, not the disease
guidedApproach.prompt: Why treat the child rather than the thermometer?
guidedApproach.guidance: Infection triggers macrophages to release interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumour necrosis factor, which raise prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus and reset the temperature set point upwards. Fever itself is rarely harmful and may help host defence; the height of the fever correlates poorly with the seriousness of the cause. What matters is the cause and the child's physiology: tachycardia, poor perfusion and lethargy signal sepsis. Young infants and malnourished children localise infection poorly, so serious bacterial infection can present with fever alone. Prolonged fever points away from common viral infection towards enteric fever, tuberculosis, abscess, Kawasaki disease, autoimmune disease or malignancy.

guidedApproach.title: Look at the child first
guidedApproach.prompt: Which features separate a sick child from a well one?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start with appearance, behaviour, colour, hydration and vital signs. Toxic appearance, lethargy or inconsolable irritability, inability to feed, dehydration, severe malnutrition, and a rash with shock or organ dysfunction are danger signs that need immediate treatment. Then search for a focus: ear, throat, chest, abdomen, urine, joints, skin and meninges. Ask about duration, contacts and season, recent travel, vaccination in the past 24 hours, and similar illness in the household. Fever beyond 5 days with conjunctival injection, red lips, rash and swollen hands suggests Kawasaki disease; an eschar suggests scrub typhus.

guidedApproach.title: Test by duration, not by habit
guidedApproach.prompt: When should a child with fever have tests?
guidedApproach.guidance: A well child with fever under 72 hours and no focus needs no investigations. After 72 hours, a blood count with differential and platelets and a peripheral smear for malaria are essential, with a rapid malaria test, dengue NS1 and IgM, blood culture and urine culture as indicated. Fever over 7 days needs a wider search: Widal only after the first week, Mantoux and Xpert for tuberculosis, HIV, autoimmune tests and imaging guided by findings. A clean-catch urine sample is desirable in children with fever without focus, especially infants. CRP or procalcitonin are optional and do not replace clinical assessment.

guidedApproach.title: Treat danger, the cause and the discomfort
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you manage a febrile child step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Manage airway, breathing, circulation and seizures first. For suspected meningitis, severe pneumonia or sepsis give a first dose of ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (100 mg/kg/day), and artesunate if severe malaria is possible, before referral. For the well child, give paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 4–6 hours, no more than 4 doses a day, to relieve discomfort rather than to normalise temperature; ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg is an option after 3 months when dengue is not suspected. Do not give antibiotics for viral fever or start empiric anti-tuberculosis treatment except for suspected TB meningitis. Teach parents the warning signs and when to return.

boardQuestions.vignette: An 18-month-old boy has fever for 4 days, no focus on examination and is drinking well. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 150/min and capillary refill under 2 seconds. He is alert between fever spikes. His mother has been giving paracetamol every 2 hours and asks for an injection to bring the fever down.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.explanation: Antibiotics are not given for fever without focus in a well child without danger signs.

options.text: Blood count, smear and platelets (urine culture desirable); correct the paracetamol to every 4–6 hours, maximum 4 doses a day
options.explanation: Correct. Fever over 72 hours without focus needs blood count, smear and platelets, with urine culture desirable; paracetamol every 2 hours risks overdose (ICMR STW; guideline).
No tests is advice only for fever under 72 hours (ICMR STW).
Widal is not useful in the first week (ICMR STW).
Empiric anti-TB treatment is only for suspected TB meningitis (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Investigate fever without focus by duration.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Over 72 hours: blood count, smear, platelets; dose paracetamol safely.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 3-year-old girl has had fever for 6 days. She has red cracked lips, bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, a polymorphous rash, swollen red hands and a 2 cm cervical lymph node. Malaria and dengue tests are negative. Platelets are 520,000/µL and CRP is raised.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Measles has cough, coryza and Koplik spots, and the rash spreads from the face.
Scarlet fever follows a streptococcal throat infection with a sandpaper rash, not this pattern.
Dengue tests are negative and dengue lowers, rather than raises, the platelets.
Correct. Fever over 5 days with conjunctival injection, lip changes, rash, extremity changes and lymphadenopathy suggests Kawasaki disease (ICMR STW).
Viral fever does not explain this cluster of mucocutaneous signs.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Recognise Kawasaki disease in prolonged fever.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Prolonged fever with mucocutaneous signs: think Kawasaki disease.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 10-month-old infant weighing 8 kg is brought with fever for 1 day. He is lethargic, will not breastfeed, has a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a non-blanching rash on the legs. Pulse is 180/min. The nearest tertiary hospital is 2 hours away.
boardQuestions.question: What should be done first?

options.explanation: This child has danger signs and needs urgent treatment.

options.text: Blood count and wait for results
options.explanation: Investigations must not delay treatment in a toxic child.

options.text: Fluid bolus and IV ceftriaxone 400 mg (50 mg/kg) before referral
options.explanation: Correct. Shock with a non-blanching rash suggests meningococcaemia; treat shock and give a first dose of ceftriaxone, then refer (ICMR STW).
Antipyretics lower temperature but do not treat shock or sepsis.
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for suspected meningococcal sepsis.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Act on danger signs in febrile infants.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Toxic child with rash and shock: treat shock, give ceftriaxone, refer.

patientEducation: Give plenty of fluids; light clothing.
Return for drowsiness, breathing difficulty, rash, poor feeding or fits.
mdtReferrals: Tertiary paediatrics for ICU needs or complex disease (ICMR STW)
dischargeCriteria: Afebrile over 48 hours or settling (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 48–72 hours if fever persists; sooner for any danger sign.

algorithms.title: Child with fever: assess, test, treat

nodes.text: Child with fever (rectal 38.0 °C or more, axillary above 37.5 °C)
Danger signs: toxic, lethargic, unable to feed, dehydrated, severe malnutrition, rash with shock?
Treat airway, shock (saline 20 mL/kg) and seizures; first dose ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (artesunate if malaria likely); admit
Neonate or young infant under 3 months?
Low threshold: full sepsis work-up (blood count, blood and urine culture, consider LP), admit and give first-dose antibiotics if unwell
Focus found on history and examination?
Treat the focus (see its topic); paracetamol for comfort
Well child: no tests; paracetamol; review if fever persists or new signs appear
Blood count, smear, platelets; add RDT, NS1/IgM, urine and blood culture as indicated
Add Widal (after 7 days), Mantoux, Xpert, HIV, autoimmune tests and imaging; refer if fever over 14 days undiagnosed
